capabilities.target: Entire user home directory (C:/Users/dev) via the filesystem MCP server, including ~/.aws/credentials and other sensitive files
Any Slack channel reachable by the bot token, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User's direct request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp's tools/list response
Response content returned by quicknotes_mcp's add_note call, round-tripped through the author's hosted sync service

controls.name: First-call tool approval, remembered as 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: The approval dialog is shown once per tool and is not re-shown on later calls ('always allow'), so it offers no protection on any call after the first, including calls carrying different and more sensitive arguments. The approval also appears to review a model-generated summary rather than raw arguments, and the injected tool description explicitly instructs the model not to surface this action to the user, which defeats that summary if the model complies. Per control_decay.md, a remembered approval is not a gate: it is recorded here but does not cover any capability's approval_gate_ref and earns no credit.

governance_refs.note: Human oversight control present but not effective after the first invocation.

controls.name: Least-privilege filesystem scope (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: Scoping fs.read_file to a dedicated, non-sensitive directory makes ~/.aws/credentials and other secrets unreachable from this agent regardless of model behavior, severing the credential-harvesting leg of the attack path.

controls.name: Tool definition pinning and hashing (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning and hashing quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions and failing closed on any change would require human review before an updated or newly poisoned description could take effect, countering MCP rug pulls. It does not retroactively fix the definition already shown in this artifact.

controls.name: System-of-record channel allowlist for Slack posts (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: Binding slack_post to a vetted, internal-only channel list sourced from configuration, not a channel name the model supplies, makes channels shared with external organizations unreachable regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Per-call raw-action approval for exfiltration-capable tools (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: A per-call approval that shows the full destination and argument contents, and is never remembered, gives a human the chance to catch a harvested-credential payload before it is sent, on every call rather than only the first.

controls.name: Injection scanning of MCP tool definitions and outputs (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier flagging imperative instructions embedded in tool descriptions or outputs would catch today's payload, but as a separate model it can be evaded by paraphrase or encoding and does not scale with a stronger primary model.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): poisoned quicknotes_mcp tool description harvests AWS credentials and exfiltrates them via add_note

attack_path.note: The add_note tool description contains an <IMPORTANT> block instructing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and place its contents in the 'context' argument, and not to mention this to the user.
fs.read_file executes against a filesystem server scoped to the entire home directory, so ~/.aws/credentials is reachable.
add_note's arguments, including the harvested credential contents, are sent to quicknotes_mcp's third-party hosted sync service, completing the exfiltration.

evidence.observation: add_note's description contains an embedded instruction, marked <IMPORTANT>, to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass its contents in the 'context' argument before calling the tool, and to hide this step from the user.
quicknotes_mcp is launched via 'npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest' with no version pin, so its tool definitions can change on every launch without review.
The filesystem MCP server is mounted at the root of the user's home directory (C:/Users/dev) rather than a scoped subdirectory, so fs.read_file can reach ~/.aws/credentials.
quicknotes_mcp is a community package published by an individual, installed with @latest on every launch.
The desktop client approves each tool only on first call and then remembers 'always allow', so later add_note calls are not reviewed at all.

recommendations.action: Scope the filesystem MCP server to a dedicated, non-sensitive directory instead of the full home directory, so credential files and SSH keys are never readable by the agent.
Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions; fail closed and require human review if the tools/list response changes between launches.
Require raw-action approval, showing full destination and arguments, on every call to add_note; remove 'always allow' memory for capabilities that can exfiltrate data.
Scan MCP tool descriptions and tool outputs for embedded imperative instructions (for example <IMPORTANT> blocks or 'do not tell the user') before they enter context.
Treat quicknotes_mcp as already compromised: rotate the AWS credentials referenced in ~/.aws/credentials and audit the account for prior unauthorized sync activity.

governance_refs.note: Supplier and third-party AI component controls.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta variant (TC1), cross-tool contamination: untrusted quicknotes_mcp output can direct exfiltration via the overly broad Slack posting scope

attack_path.note: Content returned by quicknotes_mcp's add_note call originates from, or passes through, the author's hosted sync service and must be treated as untrusted; it can carry hidden instructions the same way the tool description already does.
A hidden instruction embedded in tool output could direct the agent to read further sensitive files from the broadly-scoped home directory.
The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, providing a second, independent egress channel for exfiltrated content.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

evidence.observation: Demonstrates that quicknotes_mcp's maintainer already embeds hidden imperative instructions in content the agent ingests from this server; content returned from its calls (in.notes_output) must be assumed capable of the same.
quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its author, so content returned to the agent after a note operation originates from infrastructure the agent owner does not control.
The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, so slack_post is a broad, unscoped egress capability.
The Slack MCP server is configured with a single bot token (SLACK_BOT_TOKEN) with no indication of channel scoping.

recommendations.action: Scope the Slack bot token to a specific, internal-only set of channels and remove its ability to post to channels shared with external organizations.
Treat all content returned by quicknotes_mcp, not just its tool descriptions, as untrusted input; do not let it influence subsequent tool selection or arguments without explicit user confirmation.
Add destination confirmation for slack_post bound to a system-of-record channel list rather than a channel name the model supplies or infers.
Log and alert on any Slack post whose destination channel includes external-organization members, for post-hoc review.

rating.rationale: Both findings start from an untrusted source (an unpinned, auto-updating, individually-published third-party MCP server) reaching an irreversible egress sink carrying confidential-to-restricted data, which the base matrix rates critical before any controls. The only control present, a per-tool approval that is remembered as 'always allow' after the first call, covers no capability under rubric section 5 because a remembered approval is not a gate: it earns no credit, so residual equals inherent at critical for both findings. The filesystem server's home-directory-wide scope, the lack of any tool-definition pinning, the lack of any injection scanning, and the Slack bot's unscoped channel access mean there is no structural control left to decay, so the forecast ceiling is already reached; no plausible trigger raises the tier further, though model_upgrade and new_mcp_server would make the existing hole more reliably exploitable and would defeat ctrl.first_call_approval even further by producing more persuasive, more complete summaries or omissions at the one moment a human could intervene. ctrl.first_call_approval is the single control whose weakness most explains why nothing stands between the untrusted tool description and credential exfiltration today.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts (mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No system prompt or agent instructions artifact was provided, so the instructions review (ambiguous goals, conflicting directives, implied authority, and so on) could not be performed; this lowers confidence in any claim about the agent's own guardrails.
No access logs or audit trail artifacts were provided; detective and corrective capability could not be verified and is assumed absent.

The claim that in.notes_output (tool call output, not just the tool description) can reach cap.slack_post is inferred from general MCP tool-output-trust guidance rather than directly evidenced in the given artifacts, so find.cross_tool_slack_exfil is rated medium confidence.

The internal behavior, encryption, retention, and access controls of quicknotes_mcp's hosted sync service are unknown; data_sensitivity and consequence assume the worst case consistent with the explicit instruction to harvest AWS credentials.
